Working paper, November 2026

Listing Language and House Price Discovery

Lily Shen, Clemson University. A short guide to the paper: the question, the measure, and the main tables.

A house-price index sees a home only when its sale closes. The listing agent described the market months earlier, in the public remarks. The paper reads those remarks for three kinds of information and asks whether they show local price movements before the index does.

  • Listings with demand-heat language sell for 1.5 percent more, 9.7 days faster, and are 4.5 percentage points more likely to sell, compared within the same county-year and the same listing agent.
  • A county with one standard deviation more demand-heat language has 0.58 percentage points higher house-price growth over the next six months than other counties in the same state and month.
  • The relation belongs to the county. Reassigning the index across counties within a state and month 500 times never produces a coefficient as large.
  • Georgia is held out of the primary estimation and gives 0.43 percentage points. Pooling all three states gives 0.54 across 59 counties.

Why remarks can lead the index

The median completed listing closes 84 days after its original listing date. The mean is 104 days and the 75th percentile is 138. A closing-based index cannot observe the sale price during that interval, and a published index adds its own production lag. The remark is written when the home is first listed.

Remarks also exist for homes that never sell. In the primary sample 306,377 of 809,663 listings expire, are withdrawn, or are canceled. None of them enters a transaction-price index, and all of them enter the language measure.

The closest precedents read newspapers and social media for information that prices have not yet absorbed (Tetlock 2007; Soo 2018; Cookson et al. 2026). Listing remarks are communications of the same kind from a different source. News and social media are written by observers of a market. A remark is written by the agent selling a specific home, and that home's price later enters the index.

Data

The data are CoreLogic MLS listings in Georgia, North Carolina, and South Carolina: 2,032,935 residential listings with usable public remarks. The archive's coverage differs by state, so the design separates estimation from validation.

SampleCoverageListingsUse in the paper
PrimaryNorth and South Carolina, 2001 to 2019809,663All primary estimates. 503,286 listings sell and 306,377 do not.
Held outGeorgia, 2011 to 2021833,171Replication in a market the primary estimates never use, then a pooled table.
IndependentA separate Atlanta MLS, 2007 to 201763,085Listing-level validation with a different data source.

Each listing uses its earliest nonempty remark, assigned to the original listing month. Remarks are stable: 98.05 percent of listings have a single version of the description.

The three signals

The measure sorts phrases by the kind of information they carry, where a sentiment score would sort them by tone. “Multiple offers” describes demand for the home. “As is” describes the asset. “Motivated seller” describes the seller's constraint. All three can move price, through different channels and on different schedules.

SignalWhat it capturesRepresentative phrasesShare of listings
Demand heatCompeting buyers and fast marketsmultiple offers; highest and best; offer deadline; hot market; will not last6.9%
Seller pressureWeak-market language, price flexibility, seller urgencyback on market; price reduced; motivated seller; bring offers; relocation16.2%
Asset frictionsDistressed status, condition, financing constraintsforeclosure; short sale; REO; as is; needs work; cash only; no FHA17.1%

Shares are of all marketed listings in the primary sample. A listing can carry more than one signal.

Measurement has two steps. An LLM reads recurring expressions in their listing context and assigns them to eight predefined subcategories, which group into the three signals. Fixed scoring patterns with phrase, context, and negation guards then score every remark, so each score traces to the phrase that produced it. Discovery and scoring see the text only: no prices, outcomes, locations, or dates.

At the listing level each signal is an indicator for whether the remark carries that language. At the county-month level it is the share of listings with that language, standardized.

In North Carolina, which spans the full cycle, seller-pressure language peaks in the crisis, asset-friction language peaks in the distressed-inventory years 2009 to 2012, and demand-heat language is flat through the crisis and rises in the recovery. Georgia enters the archive in 2011 with asset-friction language on 45 percent of listings, which falls to about 15 percent as that inventory clears.

The pattern holds within the same house. With address fixed effects, demand-heat language goes with 1.5 percent higher prices and 8.5 fewer days on market across repeat listings of one home. The ordering also holds in the independent Atlanta MLS.

From listings to county prices

The county-month test regresses forward six-month growth in a hedonic house-price index on the three standardized signals. The index is built from the same MLS sales. The conventional controls are lagged six-month price growth, new listings and their growth, growth in original list prices, housing composition, and lagged failed-listing share, days on market, and sale-to-list ratio.

Primary sample: 2,090 county-months in 19 counties, North and South Carolina, 2001 to 2019. The dependent variable is forward six-month growth in the county MLS hedonic index, in log points, so 0.0058 is 0.58 percentage points. Signals are standardized county-month shares. Regressions are weighted by scored listings. Standard errors in parentheses. * p < 0.10, ** p < 0.05, *** p < 0.01.

With the full conventional set and county and month effects, demand heat is 0.41 percentage points, significant at the 10 percent level. Comparing counties within the same state and month, it is 0.58, significant at the 1 percent level, and the three signals are jointly significant with a p-value of 0.006.

Asset frictions also carry a positive coefficient, 0.55 within state-month. The paper reads this as distressed inventory moving through clearing and recovery. Seller pressure predicts weaker outcomes for its own listing and has no stable relation with county price growth.

A single favorable-minus-unfavorable index adds 0.0003 to the within R2 and is indistinguishable from zero. The three typed signals add 0.0021. Keeping the type of information is what makes the language informative.

The demand-heat path is flat for three months, reaches 0.46 percentage points at month four, and is 0.32 at month six. That is the horizon the 84-day listing-to-closing interval implies. Beyond six months the estimates are imprecise.

Is the information local?

The placebo coefficients center on zero, with a mean of 0.005 percentage points. The coefficient on the county's own index is 0.576, and no reassigned estimate is as large, which gives a randomization p-value of 0.002.

Column 2 keeps remarks whose earliest archived record is within 30 days of listing, column 3 keeps remarks archived before the listing sold or left the market, and column 4 keeps listings whose remark never changes across archived records. Standard errors in parentheses. * p < 0.10, ** p < 0.05, *** p < 0.01.

The archive's record date can reflect vendor processing, so the paper also restricts the sample by when the remark was archived. Requiring the archived record to precede the listing's sale or exit gives 0.45, significant at the 1 percent level. Listings whose remarks never change give 0.50. The sample archived within 30 days of listing is small, 879 county-months, and gives 0.21.

The paper runs two more checks on the same question. Conditioning on the cohort's own realized clearing outcomes (failed-listing share, days on market, sale-to-list ratio) moves demand heat from 0.44 to 0.38, and it is 0.56 within state-month. Subtracting each agent's own long-run rate of using each category moves it from 0.40 to 0.24, and 0.29 within state-month, where the adjusted signals remain jointly significant.

County-by-year and listing-agent fixed effects with the same controls as the primary listing-level table. Standard errors in parentheses. * p < 0.10, ** p < 0.05, *** p < 0.01.

The transaction ordering reproduces. The one difference is the demand-heat price coefficient, which is negative in Georgia: hot listings there are priced competitively, while in the Carolinas they sell at a premium.

At the county-month level, demand heat predicts 0.43 percentage points higher six-month growth in Georgia, significant at the 1 percent level, next to 0.41 in the primary sample. Vocabulary discovery read the full three-state corpus, so Georgia is out of sample for the estimated relations and in sample for the vocabulary.

Adding Georgia to the estimation sample gives 0.54 across 59 counties, with Georgia supplying 59 percent of the county-months.

Where the estimates are less precise

  • North Carolina supplies 84 percent of the primary county-months, and South Carolina's 242 cells are too few for precision on their own. The pooled table widens the base to 59 counties.
  • Holding the home fixed at the index level is hard in a two-state sample. A repeat-property index leaves 1,245 county-months in eight counties, and the demand coefficient there is close to zero. The within-home evidence comes from the listing level.
  • A holdout forecast gains in one window. Loadings estimated through 2014 lower six-month forecast RMSE by 23.5 percent in 2015 to 2019. Loadings estimated before 2007 give no gain in 2007 to 2012.

Tables and figures are from the November 2026 draft of the paper (46 pages).
